description: My name is Zakiyah, and I am a senior at the University of Washington studying Informatics (Data Science Track). I have experience working with Python, SQL, and R, as well as data visualization tools such as Tableau and Sigma, along with some frontend and backend development.
summary: FireCal PNW turns 23 years of NASA FIRMS satellite fire detections into one consistent record of burning activity for Washington and Oregon, and an interactive web dashboard built on it. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) can't be compared directly: VIIRS detects about twice as many fire pixels, so a record that switches sensors shows a fake jump in fire activity. We harmonize the two sensors by snapping both to a common 1 km daily grid and then calibrating MODIS to VIIRS-equivalent units. The calibration model was chosen from five candidates with leave-one-year-out cross-validation; on held-out years it reproduces VIIRS monthly totals within 8% and annual totals within 4%. In the dashboard, emergency managers, land managers and scientists can draw an area of interest, explore a year-by-month burning calendar, see whether any month is unusual compared with its historical median, and download CSVs. It correctly flags known extremes, such as September 2020 in the western Oregon Cascades (Labor Day fires) at 88× the usual September activity. A consistent fire history helps teams anticipate critical periods and spot abnormal seasons early.
details:
What it does FireCal PNW is a web application that answers: "When and where does the Pacific Northwest burn, and is what we're seeing now unusual?" It combines NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots from MODIS (2003–2025) and VIIRS (2012–2025) into one harmonized time series and presents it as an interactive burning activity calendar.

How it works

  1. Ingest: a Python script streams the NASA FIRMS yearly hotspot archives (~850 MB) and keeps the 1.04 million detections inside Washington and Oregon.
  2. Quality filter: only presumed vegetation fires (type 0) are kept, which removes industrial heat sources and volcanoes. Low-confidence detections are dropped (MODIS confidence < 30%, VIIRS "low").
  3. Footprint harmonization: VIIRS pixels (375 m) are about 7× smaller than MODIS pixels (1 km), so one fire produces several VIIRS detections. Both sensors are snapped to a common ~1 km grid and de-duplicated per day, giving one unit for both: "fire-pixel-days".
  4. Sensitivity calibration: even after step 3, VIIRS sees about twice as much fire activity. Using the 2012–2019 overlap, we compared five calibration models (raw, global ratio, seasonal ratio, spatial × seasonal shrinkage ratio, and log-log regression) with leave-one-year-out cross-validation. The seasonal ratio model won, with 8.1% monthly error and 4.2% annual error, versus 50% with no harmonization. We excluded 2020–2025 from calibration because the aging Terra and Aqua satellites drifted in orbit and the ratio became noisier.
  5. Harmonized record: VIIRS observations from 2012 onward; 2003–2011 MODIS converted to VIIRS-equivalent units.
  6. Dashboard: a static website (Leaflet map + Plotly charts) where users select an area (presets, a drawn rectangle or lat/lon) and a year range, then see:
    • a year × month burning calendar (counts or anomaly vs. the monthly median, with accessible color scales)
    • how any month compares with the same month in other years (multiple of the median, rank)
    • the typical fire-season profile with a typical-range band
    • raw vs. harmonized sensor totals, showing why harmonization matters
    • CSV downloads of the monthly series and of individual hotspot detections

Benefits and intended impact Emergency managers and firefighters can tell at a glance whether this month is abnormal for their area and plan for critical periods. Land managers get a consistent fire history across the switch from MODIS to VIIRS. Scientists get a documented, harmonized dataset they can download. The results match known events: August 2015 (Okanogan Complex) and September 2020 (Oregon's Labor Day fires) are the two most extreme months on record, and September 2020 in the western Oregon Cascades was 88× the usual September.

Tools and languages Python (pandas, NumPy, matplotlib) for the data pipeline, statistics and figures. JavaScript, HTML and CSS with Leaflet and Plotly.js for the dashboard. GitHub and GitHub Pages for open-source code and free hosting. No server is needed.

What makes it creative Instead of just plotting hotspots, we treated sensor harmonization as a model-selection problem and validated it the way a data scientist would: on years the model never saw. The dashboard is built around the question managers actually ask ("is this month unusual?") rather than raw counts, with a one-click anomaly view.

Factors we considered Differences in sensor resolution and sensitivity, MODIS orbit drift, filtering out non-fire heat sources, colorblind-safe color ramps, clear explanations for non-specialists, and limitations: a hotspot is a satellite thermal detection, not a burned area, and clouds or smoke can hide fires. The calibration is fit for the PNW, but the pipeline works for any region by changing one bounding box.
